newsitem.title: USA: Columbus, Ohio arena and stadium tax plan defeated.
newsitem.headline: Columbus, Ohio arena and stadium tax plan defeated.

text.p: Voters in Franklin County, Ohio, rejected a proposed 0.5 percent sales tax increase to fund a new hockey arena and soccer stadium in downtown Columbus during Tuesday's special election.
Voters rejected the sales tax plan 56 percent to 44 percent, according to unofficial election returns from the Franklin County Board of Elections.

The rejection of the sales tax likely dooms the Columbus effort to land a National Hockey League expansion franchise, but the Columbus Crew of Major League Soccer "will do whatever it can" to remain in the city, said Adam Low, a spokesman for the Crew, whose owner is also the leader of the NHL expansion bid.

"Obviously we are disappointed with what has gone on," Low said. "As far as the NHL is concerned, Lamar Hunt, our owner, who is the lead investor in the hockey team, has said this will make it impossible for the NHL to consider Columbus."
The three-year sales tax hike would have generated an estimated $203 million for construction of the two facilities, beginning on July 1.
The two facilities were expected to cost about $285 million.

Columbus is one of six U.S. cities being considered for a franchise in the next round of NHL expansion. The league has not announced how many, if any teams, it will add or decided when they would begin play.
"We have no contingency plan," Low said. "I think some people thought it would still get done regardless, but we don't know if it will get done, certainly the NHL, I would imagine, is over."
Columbus has only a fairgrounds coliseum that seats about 6,000 for hockey.

"As far as the Columbus Crew is concerned, we are here in Columbus we are committed to play in Columbus and we will do whatever we can to stay here," Low said. "If that means working something out where maybe a stadium still gets built with private funds, is that a reality, I don't know."
The Crew currently plays at the Ohio State University stadium.
The sales tax failed on a vote of 107,782 for and 138,994 against and a voter turnout of about 39 percent.
